nameStory: The American pelicanfoot gets its charming name from the distinctive flared lip of its shell that spreads out like the webbed foot of a pelican. When you look at a mature shell from the right angle, those finger-like projections really do resemble a bird's foot! The 'American' part distinguishes it from European pelican foot shells found across the Atlantic.
description: The American pelicanfoot is a medium-sized sea snail that lives in the cold waters off New England's coast. Its most striking feature is the mature shell's flared, finger-like projections that extend from the opening, giving it that distinctive pelican foot appearance. Young shells look quite different - more like typical pointed snail shells - with the characteristic foot shape only developing as they mature. These marine snails are considered among the most ancient members of their family, representing a very old lineage of sea creatures.

idTips.label: Flared Shell Lip
idTips.description: Mature shells have dramatic finger-like projections extending from the opening that feel thick and solid to the touch, resembling a webbed foot

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized conical shell with a pointed spire that feels smooth and sturdy when handled

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Typically fits comfortably in your palm, neither tiny like periwinkles nor large like whelk shells

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Usually pale cream to light brown with a somewhat chalky texture when dry

idTips.label: Juvenile Form
idTips.description: Young shells lack the flared projections and look like simple pointed snail shells with smooth, glossy surfaces

habitat: American pelicanfoot shells are found along New England's rocky coastlines and sandy beaches, typically washed up as empty shells since the living snails prefer deeper offshore waters. Look for them among tide pools and beach wrack after storms, especially along the Maine coast and other areas with cold, clean ocean water. They're most commonly discovered by beachcombers rather than observed alive, as the living snails stay in deeper waters beyond the typical shore zone.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms, often appearing clean and well-preserved among spring beach debris.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season for finding shells, though they may be more weathered from increased wave action and beach activity.
seasonality.fall: Storm season brings the best chances for finding newly washed specimens, especially after nor'easters stir up deeper waters.
seasonality.winter: Harsh storms may deposit shells high on beaches, but cold weather limits comfortable searching opportunities.

funFact: The American pelicanfoot represents one of the most ancient shell designs still alive today - scientists consider it the most primitive member of its entire family, making each shell you find a living fossil that has barely changed its form for millions of years!
confusionNotes: Young American pelicanfoot shells without their characteristic projections can be confused with common periwinkles or other pointed snails, but they're noticeably larger and lack the dark banding typical of periwinkles. Remember: if it doesn't have the 'pelican foot' flare, it might be a juvenile or a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Many beachcombers find broken or partial shells and don't realize they've discovered a pelicanfoot because the distinctive projections are fragile and often break off. Even a shell missing some of its 'toes' is still identifiable by the thick, flared lip area where the projections attach.
compareHints: The American pelicanfoot is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique in the region. Compared to other pelican foot snails worldwide, it's distinguished by its specific projection pattern and size. No other local shells develop the same dramatic flared, finger-like extensions from their openings.
